Binary Classification Model on Hotel Cancellation Probability¶

Data cleaning and predictive modelling on Lisbon hotel booking records, predicting whether a reservation will be cancelled before arrival.

I use VS Code with the Python (ms-python.python), Python Environments (ms-python.vscode-python-envs), and Jupyter (ms-toolsai.jupyter) extensions. The Python Environments extension activates .venv in the integrated terminal on its own, so there is nothing to source.

Setup¶

Clone into your empty working directory:

git clone https://codeberg.org/daraknet/Lisbon.git .

Python is pinned to 3.12.14 in .python-version and mise.toml.

With mise (what I use)¶

mise trust
mise install      # installs Python 3.12.14
mise run install  # creates and activates .venv & installs dependencies

If mise run install fails, install the dependencies directly:

python -m pip install --no-cache-dir -U -r requirements.txt --prefer-binary

With uv (recommended)¶

uv is becoming the standard for Python project management. It installs the interpreter, creates the venv, and installs packages in one step. See https://docs.astral.sh/uv/

uv sync

Without either¶

Install Python 3.12.14 however you prefer — pyenv, asdf, or python.org.

python3 -m venv .venv
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

VS Code¶

Open the folder and select ./.venv/bin/python as the interpreter (Command Palette → Python: Select Interpreter). It normally prompts on its own.

Outside VS Code, activate manually: source .venv/bin/activate (.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 on Windows).

Part 1 — Exploratory data analysis¶

The real-world problem. Cancellations cost the hotel chain money: a cancelled room may go unsold, staffing and purchasing are planned against expected occupancy, and overbooking policies depend on knowing how much attrition to expect. If we can estimate the cancellation risk of each booking at the moment it is made, the hotel can act early — ask for a deposit, send confirmation nudges, oversell selectively, or prioritise waitlists.

The machine-learning framing. This is a binary classification problem: one row per booking, target IsCanceled (1 = the booking was later cancelled). The model must output a probability, not just a label, because different business actions have different thresholds (a confirmation email is cheap; denying a room is not).

The information constraint that shapes everything. The prediction is made when the customer books. Every feature must be knowable at that moment. This rules out several columns and whole data sources, which I identify during EDA and formally drop in Part 2 (the leakage audit).

What this means for metrics (justified in detail in Part 4): the classes are imbalanced (~37% cancelled), so plain accuracy is misleading — always predicting "not cancelled" scores 63%. I evaluate with ROC-AUC (how well the model ranks risky bookings above safe ones), precision/recall at an operating threshold (what the hotel experiences when it acts on the flag), and calibration (whether a predicted 70% risk really cancels ~70% of the time — necessary if the probability drives decisions).

1.1 First look: the target and where the two hotels differ¶

IsCanceled is the target. Before any modelling I want to know: how common are cancellations, do the two hotels behave differently, and which variables move the rate?

1.2 Lead time: the single strongest signal¶

Lead time is the number of days between making the booking and arrival. Intuition says a booking made a year out has far more opportunity to fall through than one made yesterday

  • and the data agrees strongly.
In [6]:

lt_rate = bookings.groupby(lt_bins, observed=True).IsCanceled.mean()

1.3 Market segment and deposit type¶

Two more strong, business-meaningful drivers. The deposit result looks paradoxical at first sight - non-refundable bookings cancel 99% of the time - so it deserves a closer look rather than blind acceptance.

In [7]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [3, 2]})

seg = (bookings.assign(m=bookings.MarketSegment.str.strip())
       .groupby("m").IsCanceled.agg(["mean", "count"])
       .query("count >= 100").sort_values("mean"))
axes[0].barh(seg.index, seg["mean"], color=C_BLUE, height=0.6)
for y, (r, n) in enumerate(zip(seg["mean"], seg["count"])):
    axes[0].annotate(f" {r:.0%}  (n={n:,})", (r, y), va="center", fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_title("Group bookings are the riskiest segment")
axes[0].set_xlim(0, 0.78)
axes[0].xaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}")

dep = (bookings.assign(d=bookings.DepositType.str.strip())
       .groupby("d").IsCanceled.agg(["mean", "count"]).sort_values("mean"))
axes[1].barh(dep.index, dep["mean"], color=C_BLUE, height=0.5)
for y, (r, n) in enumerate(zip(dep["mean"], dep["count"])):
    axes[1].annotate(f" {r:.0%}  (n={n:,})", (r, y), va="center", fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_title("The non-refund paradox")
axes[1].set_xlim(0, 1.32)
axes[1].xaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}")
plt.show()

Why would customers who paid a non-refundable deposit cancel 99% of the time? This is a known quirk of this dataset, and the payments log (Part 2) confirms the deposits were genuinely charged. The accepted explanation (Antonio et al., 2019) is that these are dominated by block reservations from particular markets - often speculative bookings made in bulk (e.g. to obtain visas or to hold inventory) with no real intention to stay, where the deposit terms were part of an agent agreement rather than a sign of commitment. The practical consequence for us: DepositType is a legitimately predictive booking-time feature, but it is a proxy for a booking channel behaviour, not a psychological signal of commitment - worth remembering when interpreting the model.

1.4 Bookings over time¶

Both volume and cancellation rate drift over the two years - the city hotel grows and its cancellation rate trends upward. This motivates the time-based train/test split used in Part 3: a model deployed in production predicts the future, so it should be tested on a later period than it was trained on. (Two stacked panels, one measure each - never a dual-axis chart.)

In [8]:
MONTH_NUM = {m: i for i, m in enumerate(
    ["January", "February", "March", "April", "May", "June", "July",
     "August", "September", "October", "November", "December"], 1)}
bookings["arrival_date"] = pd.to_datetime(dict(
    year=bookings.ArrivalDateYear,
    month=bookings.ArrivalDateMonth.map(MONTH_NUM),
    day=bookings.ArrivalDateDayOfMonth))
bookings["booking_date"] = bookings.arrival_date - pd.to_timedelta(bookings.LeadTime, unit="D")

monthly = (bookings.set_index("arrival_date")
           .groupby([pd.Grouper(freq="MS"), "hotel"]).IsCanceled
           .agg(n="size", rate="mean").reset_index())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8.5, 5), sharex=True)
for hotel, grp in monthly.groupby("hotel"):
    axes[0].plot(grp.arrival_date, grp.n, color=HOTEL_COLOR[hotel], lw=2, label=hotel)
    axes[1].plot(grp.arrival_date, grp.rate, color=HOTEL_COLOR[hotel], lw=2, label=hotel)
axes[0].set_title("Monthly arrivals by hotel")
axes[0].set_ylabel("bookings")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)
axes[1].set_title("Monthly cancellation rate by hotel")
axes[1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}")
axes[1].set_ylabel("share cancelled")
axes[1].legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

1.5 EDA takeaways¶

  • ~37% of bookings cancel; the city hotel (42%) more than the resort (28%).
  • Lead time is strongly and monotonically related to cancellation (12% for last-minute bookings up to ~57% for bookings 6+ months out).
  • Deposit type: "Non Refund" bookings cancel 99% of the time (see the paradox note).
  • Market segment: Groups cancel 61%; Direct and Corporate bookings ~15-19%.
  • Volume and cancellation rates drift over time, so evaluation must respect time order.
  • Data quality issues spotted along the way (padded strings, disguised NULLs, impossible ages, leaky columns) are inventoried and fixed in Part 2.

1.6 A non-ML baseline heuristic¶

Any ML model must beat a rule a hotel manager could implement in a spreadsheet, or it is not worth deploying. From the two strongest EDA signals I define:

Flag a booking as "will cancel" if the deposit type is Non Refund, or the lead time exceeds 100 days.

The threshold of 100 days is roughly where the decile curve in 1.2 crosses a 45% cancellation rate. I also define a graded version (heuristic_score) so the heuristic can be compared with the models on ranking metrics (ROC-AUC) as well: it orders bookings by lead time and puts all Non-Refund bookings on top. Both are evaluated properly on the held-out test period in Part 4 - defining them here, before modelling, keeps the comparison honest.

In [9]:
def heuristic_flag(t: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    """Binary rule: Non-Refund deposit or lead time > 100 days -> predict cancel."""
    return ((t.DepositType.str.strip() == "Non Refund") | (t.LeadTime > 100)).astype(int)

def heuristic_score(t: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    """Graded version for ranking metrics: lead time, with Non-Refund forced on top."""
    return t.LeadTime + 1000 * (t.DepositType.str.strip() == "Non Refund")

flag = heuristic_flag(bookings)
print(f"Heuristic flags {flag.mean():.1%} of all bookings")
print(f"In-sample precision {bookings.IsCanceled[flag == 1].mean():.1%}, "
      f"recall {flag[bookings.IsCanceled == 1].mean():.1%} "
      f"(proper out-of-time evaluation follows in Part 4)")

Heuristic flags 42.6% of all bookings
In-sample precision 54.4%, recall 62.6% (proper out-of-time evaluation follows in Part 4)

Part 2 - Data cleaning and feature engineering¶

2.1 Inventory of data-quality issues¶

Everything below was discovered (the checks are in the cells that follow), not assumed:

# Issue Where Fix
1 Categorical values padded with trailing/leading spaces (e.g. "BB ") H1/H2: Meal, DepositType, room types, Agent, Company strip whitespace on all string columns
2 Missing values disguised as the string "NULL" Agent (~16k), Company (~112k) convert to real missing; encode as has_agent/has_company flags
3 Children has 4 NaN H1/H2 fill with 0 (mode; a missing count of children means none were recorded)
4 Meal = "Undefined" (1,169) H1/H2 map to SC - the data dictionary of the source dataset defines Undefined and SC as the same thing (no meal package)
5 One negative ADR (-6.38) and one extreme ADR (5400) H2 negative -> 0 (a price cannot be negative); the 5400 is kept - it is a real booking and tree models are robust to it
6 180 bookings with 0 adults + 0 children + 0 babies H1/H2 dropped - a room with no occupants is not a valid stay record
7 Duplicate guest rows (1,068 ids appear twice: UPPERCASE name + missing age) Guests deduplicate keeping the most complete row per guest
8 Impossible ages: -1 (234), >100 (325), NaN (1,587) Guests treat as missing; models handle missing age natively / via imputation
9 Country coded inconsistently: ISO-3 mostly, but CN/cn for China Guests + H1/H2 normalise to upper-case ISO-3 (CN -> CHN)
10 Payment timestamps in dd/mm/yyyy format (other files use ISO) Payments parse with explicit format
11 Weather dates in mixed formats, location spelled 6 ways Weather shown in 2.5 - the file is excluded on more fundamental grounds
12 Leakage columns - values that only exist after the outcome several the leakage audit in 2.7 drops them with reasons
In [10]:
bk = bookings.copy()

# (1) strip padding from every string column
str_cols = [c for c in bk.columns if bk[c].dtype == object or str(bk[c].dtype) in ("str", "string")]
for c in str_cols:
    bk[c] = bk[c].str.strip()

# (2) "NULL" strings -> real missing
n_null_agent, n_null_comp = bk.Agent.eq("NULL").sum(), bk.Company.eq("NULL").sum()
bk[["Agent", "Company"]] = bk[["Agent", "Company"]].replace("NULL", pd.NA)

# (3) missing Children -> 0
bk["Children"] = bk.Children.fillna(0).astype(int)

# (4) Undefined meal == SC per the source data dictionary
n_undef_meal = bk.Meal.eq("Undefined").sum()
bk["Meal"] = bk.Meal.replace("Undefined", "SC")

# (5) negative price -> 0
n_neg_adr = (bk.ADR < 0).sum()
bk.loc[bk.ADR < 0, "ADR"] = 0.0

# (6) bookings with nobody travelling
no_guests = (bk.Adults + bk.Children + bk.Babies) == 0
bk = bk[~no_guests].copy()

# (9) country: CN/cn -> CHN, everything upper-case
bk["Country"] = bk.Country.str.upper().replace("CN", "CHN")

print(f"NULL-string agents: {n_null_agent:,} | NULL-string companies: {n_null_comp:,}")
print(f"Undefined meals remapped: {n_undef_meal:,} | negative ADR fixed: {n_neg_adr}")
print(f"Zero-occupant bookings dropped: {no_guests.sum()} -> {len(bk):,} bookings remain")

NULL-string agents: 16,340 | NULL-string companies: 112,593
Undefined meals remapped: 1,169 | negative ADR fixed: 1
Zero-occupant bookings dropped: 180 -> 119,210 bookings remain

2.2 Cleaning the guest profiles¶

Duplicates here are not identical rows: each duplicated guest id has one normal row and one with an UPPER-CASE name and a missing age (a classic double-entry artefact). Sorting so the most complete row comes first and keeping that one resolves all of them without losing information.

In [11]:
gu = guests.copy()
for c in ["name", "country", "email", "notes"]:
    gu[c] = gu[c].str.strip()

dup_ids = gu.guest_id.duplicated().sum()
gu = (gu.assign(_missing=gu.isna().sum(axis=1))
        .sort_values(["guest_id", "_missing"])
        .drop_duplicates("guest_id", keep="first")
        .drop(columns="_missing"))

# impossible ages -> missing (nobody is -1 or 999 years old)
bad_age = (gu.age < 16) | (gu.age > 100)
print(f"Duplicate guest ids resolved: {dup_ids:,}")
print(f"Impossible ages set to missing: {bad_age.sum():,} "
      f"(range was {guests.age.min():.0f} to {guests.age.max():.0f})")
gu.loc[bad_age, "age"] = np.nan

gu["country"] = gu.country.str.upper().replace("CN", "CHN")
print(f"Guests after cleaning: {len(gu):,} | every booking has a guest profile: "
      f"{bk.GuestID.isin(gu.guest_id).all()}")

Duplicate guest ids resolved: 1,068
Impossible ages set to missing: 564 (range was -1 to 999)
Guests after cleaning: 106,828 | every booking has a guest profile: True

The notes column is a leak - here is the proof¶

Some notes say things like "Has cancelled a previous reservation", and bookings by guests with such notes cancel 75% of the time versus 34% for everyone else. Tempting feature! But the notes have no timestamp, so I checked when they could have been written: 6,511 guests with a cancellation note have exactly one booking in the entire dataset - there is no "previous reservation" for the note to refer to. For 76% of them that single booking is the one that got cancelled. The note describes the very outcome we are predicting, i.e. the profile text was written (or updated) after the outcome. Using it would leak the future, so notes is excluded from the features. The honest replacement is to compute each guest's real cancellation history from the booking tables, using only what was known before the booking date - done in 2.6.

In [12]:
note_cancel = gu.set_index("guest_id").notes.str.lower().str.contains("cancel", na=False)
per_guest = bk.groupby("GuestID").agg(n_bookings=("BookingID", "count"),
                                      n_cancelled=("IsCanceled", "sum"))
per_guest["note"] = per_guest.index.map(note_cancel)

with_note = bk.GuestID.map(note_cancel)
print("Cancellation rate by presence of a cancellation-mentioning note:")
print(bk.groupby(with_note).IsCanceled.agg(rate="mean", n="count").round(3), "\n")

single = per_guest[per_guest.n_bookings == 1]
noted = single[single.note]
print(f"Guests with a cancellation note but only ONE booking ever: {len(noted):,}")
print(f"...whose single booking was cancelled: {noted.n_cancelled.gt(0).mean():.1%} "
      f"(vs {single.n_cancelled.gt(0).mean():.1%} across all single-booking guests)")
print("=> the notes are written after the fact: excluded as target leakage")

2.3 Payment events: two usable signals, two leaks¶

The payment log has four event types. The question for each is the same: does this event exist at the moment the booking is made?

  • deposit_authorised and card_declined happen at/around booking time (every decline in the data occurs within 3 days of the booking date) - usable.
  • payment_received is charged at the stay, so it exists only for bookings that were never cancelled - its presence is the answer key (0% cancellation).
  • refund_issued happens because of a cancellation (100% cancellation) - also the answer key.

The table below establishes this empirically. One more check: deposit_authorised turns out to be almost perfectly redundant with DepositType != "No Deposit" (it is the payment log's mirror of the same fact), so the only new information kept is the number of card declines, which is genuinely predictive: bookings with a declined card cancel 67% of the time versus 37% overall.

In [13]:
pay = payments.copy()
pay["event_time"] = pd.to_datetime(pay.event_time, format="%d/%m/%Y %H:%M")

ev = pay.pivot_table(index="booking_id", columns="event_type",
                     values="amount", aggfunc="count").fillna(0)
audit = bk.set_index("BookingID")[["IsCanceled", "booking_date", "DepositType"]].join(ev)
audit[ev.columns] = audit[ev.columns].fillna(0)

rows = []
for e in ev.columns:
    present = audit[audit[e] > 0]
    rows.append({"event": e, "bookings with event": len(present),
                 "cancellation rate when present": round(present.IsCanceled.mean(), 3)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nOverall cancellation rate: {bk.IsCanceled.mean():.3f}")

# decline timing: all within days of booking -> knowable at/just after booking time
declines = pay[pay.event_type == "card_declined"].merge(
    bk[["BookingID", "booking_date"]], left_on="booking_id", right_on="BookingID")
delta = (declines.event_time - declines.booking_date).dt.days
print(f"\ncard_declined events occur {delta.min()}-{delta.max()} days after booking")

# deposit_authorised is redundant with DepositType
print("\ndeposit_authorised vs DepositType (crosstab):")
print(pd.crosstab(audit["deposit_authorised"] > 0, audit.DepositType))

pay_features = ev[["card_declined"]].rename(columns={"card_declined": "n_card_declined"})

2.4 Weather: establishing that a source adds no value¶

The brief allows dropping a source if you show how you established that. Two independent reasons:

1. The information does not exist at prediction time. The model predicts at booking time; the median lead time is 69 days and 75% of bookings are made more than two weeks ahead. Weather is not forecastable beyond ~10 days, so arrival-day weather is unknowable for the overwhelming majority of bookings. Joining it to the training table would train the model on information it can never have in production.

2. Even cheating, there is next to no signal. As a falsification test I join arrival-day weather anyway (as if we had a perfect oracle) and check whether it separates cancelled from kept bookings. Rainfall is uninformative (AUC 0.50 - two thirds of readings are 0mm, so terciles even collapse). Temperature shows a mild gradient (33% to 40% across terciles, AUC 0.53), but that is just seasonality wearing a disguise - warm days are summer days, and the arrival month already carries that information at booking time. Weather adds nothing beyond features we legitimately have.

The file is also the dirtiest of the five (mixed date formats, six spellings of two locations, duplicate readings, a 83.7°C "maximum temperature") - documented below for completeness, but the exclusion stands on the two arguments above, which no amount of cleaning fixes.

In [14]:
wt = weather.copy()
print("Location spellings found:", sorted(wt.location.unique()))
iso_mask = wt.date.str.match(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}")
print(f"Date formats: {iso_mask.sum():,} ISO (yyyy-mm-dd) vs {(~iso_mask).sum():,} dd/mm/yyyy")

wt["location"] = wt.location.str.strip().str.title()
wt["date"] = pd.to_datetime(np.where(iso_mask, wt.date, pd.NA), errors="coerce")
wt2 = wt.copy()
wt2.loc[wt2.date.isna(), "date"] = pd.to_datetime(
    weather.date[~iso_mask], format="%d/%m/%Y", errors="coerce")
print(f"Duplicate (date, location) readings after normalising: "
      f"{wt2.duplicated(['date', 'location']).sum()}")
wt2 = wt2.drop_duplicates(["date", "location"])

print(f"\n75% of bookings are made {bk.LeadTime.quantile(0.25):.0f}+ days ahead "
      f"(median {bk.LeadTime.median():.0f}) - far beyond any forecast horizon")

# --- falsification test: join arrival-day weather as if we had a perfect oracle
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

oracle = bk.assign(location=bk.hotel.map(loc_map)).merge(

2.5 Guest history features (time-aware)¶

What a repeat guest did before is legitimately knowable at booking time - the trick is computing it without peeking. For each booking I count, over that guest's other bookings:

  • prior_bookings - bookings made before this one (booking_date strictly earlier);
  • prior_cancellations - prior bookings whose cancellation was already known before this booking was made (a cancellation becomes known on its ReservationStatusDate, so I compare that date, not the arrival date, against the current booking date);
  • prior_cancel_rate - cancellations over resolved prior bookings (0 for first-timers).

This is the honest version of what the leaky notes column pretended to offer. Only ~10% of bookings come from repeat guests, so the loop over repeat guests is cheap.

In [15]:
bk["outcome_known"] = pd.to_datetime(bk.ReservationStatusDate)

prior_b = np.zeros(len(bk)); prior_c = np.zeros(len(bk)); prior_res = np.zeros(len(bk))
pos = {bid: i for i, bid in enumerate(bk.BookingID)}
repeats = bk[bk.GuestID.duplicated(keep=False)]
for gid, gdf in repeats.groupby("GuestID"):
    bd = gdf.booking_date.to_numpy()
    known = gdf.outcome_known.to_numpy()
    canc = gdf.IsCanceled.to_numpy()
    ids = gdf.BookingID.to_numpy()
    for i in range(len(gdf)):
        j = pos[ids[i]]
        prior_b[j] = (bd < bd[i]).sum()
        resolved = known < bd[i]
        prior_res[j] = resolved.sum()
        prior_c[j] = (resolved & (canc == 1)).sum()

bk["prior_bookings"] = prior_b
bk["prior_cancellations"] = prior_c
bk["prior_cancel_rate"] = np.where(prior_res > 0, prior_c / np.maximum(prior_res, 1), 0.0)

rep_mask = bk.prior_bookings > 0
print(f"Bookings from guests with a prior booking: {rep_mask.sum():,} ({rep_mask.mean():.1%})")
print("\nCancellation rate by prior history (sanity check that the feature is meaningful):")
print(bk.groupby(np.select([~rep_mask, bk.prior_cancellations == 0], ["first booking", "prior, never cancelled"], "prior cancellation"))
        .IsCanceled.agg(rate="mean", n="count").round(3))

2.6 The modelling table: joins and the leakage audit¶

Joins. Guests join 1:1 on GuestID (only cleaned age survives - name and email are identifiers, notes is leakage, guest country duplicates the booking's own Country). Payments aggregate to one row per booking (count of card declines; missing = 0 declines). Weather is excluded (2.4). Guest history comes from the booking tables themselves (2.5).

The audit. Each original column is kept or dropped with a reason. The dropped ones:

Column Reason for dropping
ReservationStatus, ReservationStatusDate they are the outcome (Canceled / Check-Out and when)
AssignedRoomType assigned at check-in, after the prediction moment (kept: ReservedRoomType, chosen at booking)
BookingChanges accumulates edits made after booking
DaysInWaitingList resolved between booking and confirmation - not knowable at the moment of booking
Agent, Company raw ids have hundreds of levels and would overfit; replaced by has_agent / has_company flags
ArrivalDateYear, ArrivalDateWeekNumber, ArrivalDateDayOfMonth year would not generalise to future years; month captures the seasonal signal
guest name, email, notes identifiers / leakage (2.2)
payments payment_received, refund_issued mirror the outcome (2.3)
weather (whole file) not knowable at booking time + no signal (2.4)

Part 3 - Model building¶

3.1 Train/test split: out-of-time, because production predicts the future¶

A deployed model scores future bookings using patterns learned from the past, and 1.4 showed both volume and cancellation behaviour drift over the two years. A random split would let the model train on March 2017 and be tested on February 2017 - flattering and unrealistic. So I hold out the last six months of arrivals (from 1 March 2017) as the test set and never touch it until Part 4.

Two subtleties worth stating:

  • Repeat guests appear on both sides of the split (about 10% of bookings). This is not leakage - it is exactly the production situation (a known guest books again) - and the guest-history features were built time-aware in 2.5, so nothing from the future crosses the boundary.
  • Hyperparameter tuning happens with stratified 3-fold cross-validation inside the training window only; the out-of-time test set is reserved for the final comparison.

3.2 Two model families¶

  • Regularised logistic regression - a strong, fast, interpretable linear baseline. Needs imputation (median age), scaling, and one-hot encoding; rare categories (fewer than 100 bookings) are folded into an "infrequent" bucket so country codes seen a handful of times do not become noise coefficients. Tuned: regularisation strength C and whether to reweight classes.
  • Histogram gradient-boosted trees (HistGradientBoostingClassifier) - a different family entirely: non-linear, learns feature interactions (e.g. lead time x market segment), handles missing age natively and treats categoricals natively without one-hot blow-up. Tuned: learning rate, tree size, leaf regularisation.

scikit-learn is sufficient for both; both live inside a single Pipeline, so the exact preprocessing travels with the model into the Part 5 scoring artefact.

In [17]:
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder, OrdinalEncoder
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, RandomizedSearchCV, StratifiedKFold
from scipy.stats import loguniform

TEST_START = pd.Timestamp("2017-03-01")
train = model_df[model_df.arrival_date < TEST_START]
test  = model_df[model_df.arrival_date >= TEST_START]
X_train, y_train = train[NUM_FEATURES + CAT_FEATURES], train[TARGET]
X_test,  y_test  = test[NUM_FEATURES + CAT_FEATURES],  test[TARGET]
print(f"train: {len(train):,} bookings (arrivals Jul 2015 - Feb 2017), "
      f"cancellation rate {y_train.mean():.1%}")
print(f"test:  {len(test):,} bookings (arrivals Mar - Aug 2017), "
      f"cancellation rate {y_test.mean():.1%}")

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

In [18]:
# --- Model family 1: regularised logistic regression -------------------------
logreg = Pipeline([
    ("prep", ColumnTransformer([
        ("num", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                          ("scale", StandardScaler())]), NUM_FEATURES),
        ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist",
                              min_frequency=100), CAT_FEATURES),
    ])),
    ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)),
])
lr_search = GridSearchCV(
    logreg,
    {"clf__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10], "clf__class_weight": [None, "balanced"]},
    cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1)
lr_search.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(f"best params: {lr_search.best_params_}")
print(f"cross-validated ROC-AUC on train: {lr_search.best_score_:.4f}")

best params: {'clf__C': 1, 'clf__class_weight': 'balanced'}
cross-validated ROC-AUC on train: 0.9138
In [19]:
# --- Model family 2: histogram gradient-boosted trees ------------------------
# OrdinalEncoder maps categories to integers; unknown categories at scoring time
# become NaN, which the trees treat as "missing" - a graceful production behaviour.
hgb = Pipeline([
    ("prep", ColumnTransformer([
        ("cat", OrdinalEncoder(handle_unknown="use_encoded_value",
                               unknown_value=np.nan), CAT_FEATURES),
        ("num", "passthrough", NUM_FEATURES),
    ])),
    ("clf", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
        categorical_features=list(range(len(CAT_FEATURES))),
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE)),
])
hgb_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    hgb,
    {"clf__learning_rate": loguniform(0.03, 0.3),
     "clf__max_leaf_nodes": [15, 31, 63],
     "clf__min_samples_leaf": [20, 50, 100],
     "clf__l2_regularization": loguniform(1e-3, 1.0),
     "clf__max_iter": [200, 400]},
    n_iter=12, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
hgb_search.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(f"best params: {hgb_search.best_params_}")
print(f"cross-validated ROC-AUC on train: {hgb_search.best_score_:.4f}")

3.3 What did the models learn - and does it match the EDA?¶

Before trusting either model I check that what drives its predictions is consistent with Part 1. For the linear model I read the coefficients directly (they are log-odds per standard deviation for numeric features); for the boosted trees I use permutation importance on held-out data (how much AUC drops when a feature is shuffled).

In [20]:
import re
coef = pd.Series(
    lr_search.best_estimator_["clf"].coef_[0],
    index=lr_search.best_estimator_["prep"].get_feature_names_out())
coef.index = [re.sub(r"^(num|cat)__", "", i) for i in coef.index]
top = pd.concat([coef.nlargest(9), coef.nsmallest(9)]).sort_values()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.6))
ax.barh(top.index, top.values,
        color=[C_ORANGE if v > 0 else C_BLUE for v in top.values], height=0.65)
ax.axvline(0, color="0.3", lw=0.8)
ax.set_title("Logistic regression: strongest drivers of cancellation risk")
ax.set_xlabel("coefficient (log-odds; orange pushes toward cancel, blue away)")
plt.show()
In [21]:
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
rng_sample = test.sample(min(20000, len(test)), random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
perm = permutation_importance(
    hgb_search.best_estimator_, rng_sample[NUM_FEATURES + CAT_FEATURES],
    rng_sample[TARGET], scoring="roc_auc", n_repeats=5,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1)
imp = pd.Series(perm.importances_mean, index=NUM_FEATURES + CAT_FEATURES).nlargest(12)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.barh(imp.index[::-1], imp.values[::-1], color=C_BLUE, height=0.65)
ax.set_title("Boosted trees: permutation importance (AUC lost when shuffled)")
ax.set_xlabel("mean AUC decrease over 5 shuffles")
plt.show()

Both models agree with the EDA, which is reassuring: lead time, deposit type and country/market segment dominate, with the guest-history features (prior_cancel_rate) and special requests (engaged customers cancel less) close behind. Nothing important looks like an artefact - if, say, n_card_declined had come out as the single dominant feature, that would have warranted a leakage re-check.

Part 4 - Evaluation¶

4.1 Metric choice, justified¶

  • ROC-AUC - threshold-free ranking quality: the probability a random cancelled booking scores higher than a random kept one. Good headline metric, comparable across models and the graded heuristic.
  • PR-AUC (average precision) - focuses on the positive (cancelled) class; more informative than ROC-AUC when classes are imbalanced and the positive class is what the hotel acts on.
  • Precision / recall / F1 at an operating threshold - what the hotel actually experiences: of the bookings we flag, how many really cancel (precision - wasted interventions when wrong), and how many of the true cancellations we catch (recall - missed revenue protection when wrong).
  • Brier score & calibration curve - whether the predicted probabilities are honest frequencies, which matters because Part 5 outputs a probability for downstream decisions, not just a flag.
  • Plain accuracy is reported only for completeness: predicting "nobody cancels" already scores 61% on the test period.

The operating threshold is not tuned on the test set: I pick it by maximising F1 on out-of-fold predictions within the training window, then apply it once to the test set.

In [22]:
from sklearn.metrics import (roc_auc_score, average_precision_score, brier_score_loss,
                             precision_score, recall_score, f1_score, accuracy_score,
                             roc_curve, precision_recall_curve)
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict
from sklearn.base import clone

p_lr  = lr_search.best_estimator_.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
p_hgb = hgb_search.best_estimator_.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
heur_test = test.assign(DepositType=test.DepositType.astype(str))
h_flag  = heuristic_flag(heur_test)
h_score = heuristic_score(heur_test)

# operating threshold: chosen on out-of-fold train predictions, never on test
winner_name, winner_search = max(
    [("logistic regression", lr_search), ("gradient boosting", hgb_search)],
    key=lambda kv: roc_auc_score(y_test, kv[1].best_estimator_.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]))
oof = cross_val_predict(clone(winner_search.best_estimator_), X_train, y_train,
                        cv=cv, method="predict_proba", n_jobs=-1)[:, 1]
grid = np.round(np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 181), 3)
f1s = [f1_score(y_train, oof >= t) for t in grid]
THRESHOLD = float(grid[int(np.argmax(f1s))])
print(f"strongest model on test ROC-AUC: {winner_name}")
print(f"operating threshold (max F1 on train out-of-fold): {THRESHOLD:.2f}")

def row(name, y, score=None, flag=None):
    r = {"model": name}
    if score is not None:
        flag = (score >= THRESHOLD).astype(int)
        r |= {"ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(y, score),
              "PR-AUC": average_precision_score(y, score),
              "Brier": brier_score_loss(y, score)}
    else:
        r |= {"ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(y, flag), "PR-AUC": np.nan, "Brier": np.nan}
    r |= {"precision": precision_score(y, flag, zero_division=0),
          "recall": recall_score(y, flag), "F1": f1_score(y, flag),
          "accuracy": accuracy_score(y, flag)}
    return r

results = pd.DataFrame([
    row("always 'no cancel'", y_test, flag=np.zeros(len(y_test), dtype=int)),
    row("heuristic (Part 1 rule)", y_test, flag=h_flag.values),
    row("logistic regression", y_test, score=p_lr),
    row("gradient boosting", y_test, score=p_hgb),
]).set_index("model")
# ranking metrics for the graded heuristic
results.loc["heuristic (Part 1 rule)", "ROC-AUC"] = roc_auc_score(y_test, h_score)
results.loc["heuristic (Part 1 rule)", "PR-AUC"] = average_precision_score(y_test, h_score)
results.round(3)

4.3 What the comparison means for the real-world use case¶

  • Both ML models clearly beat the heuristic on every metric (ROC-AUC ~0.90 vs 0.71, precision at comparable recall ~0.77-0.82 vs 0.51). The heuristic is still not useless - it catches two thirds of cancellations with two if-statements - and that is exactly why it is the right yardstick: a model that could not beat it would not justify an ML system's operational cost.
  • The most instructive result is the one between the two models. In cross-validation the boosted trees looked far stronger (0.957 vs 0.914), but on the out-of-time test both land at ~0.90. Random CV folds let the trees exploit patterns local to the training period (specific country/segment/time pockets), and that advantage evaporated when predicting a genuinely later period - precisely the situation the model faces in production, and the reason the split in 3.1 was time-based. Had I model-selected on CV alone I would have shipped an oversold model.
  • Given effectively tied discrimination, the logistic regression is the better production choice: marginally better calibrated (Brier 0.125 vs 0.129), far simpler to explain to hotel operations ("long lead time + non-refund channel + this country mix = risk"), and cheaper to serve and retrain. That is the model serialised in Part 5.
  • The probabilities are well calibrated, so the hotel can treat the score as an actual risk: rank tomorrow's bookings, size an overbooking buffer by summing probabilities, or trigger different actions in different bands (above ~0.8 request a deposit or call to confirm; 0.5-0.8 a friendly confirmation email; below 0.5 nothing).
  • Honest caveats: performance is measured on one six-month future window of the same two hotels; the Non-Refund/Groups behaviour is a channel phenomenon that could change abruptly if agent contracts change (a reason for the monitoring in Part 5); and new guests are ranked on booking attributes alone, since they have no history yet.

Part 5 - Production¶

5.1 The scoring artefact¶

For deployment I refit the winning pipeline (preprocessing + model, same hyperparameters) on all labelled data - once evaluation is done, holding back the test months would just waste the freshest six months of behaviour. Everything the scoring service needs is written to artifacts/:

  • model.joblib - the fitted sklearn pipeline (preprocessing travels inside it);
  • metadata.json - feature lists, operating threshold, training window, versions;
  • guest_lookup.csv - guest id -> cleaned age;
  • booking_history.csv - the minimal per-booking history (booking date, outcome, when the outcome became known) from which the scorer rebuilds prior_bookings, prior_cancellations and prior_cancel_rate for a returning guest - with the same time-aware logic as 2.5.

5.2 Scoring one new booking¶

score_booking.py (in the repository root) ingests a single JSON record containing only what exists at booking time - the booking fields plus the guest's id - looks up the guest's age and time-aware history from the artefact tables, assembles the exact feature row the pipeline expects, and prints the probability and decision. booking.json is a ready-to-run sample instance. Note what is absent from the input: no reservation status, no payment outcomes, no weather - the scorer physically cannot leak because the production interface only accepts booking-time fields.

5.3 Running this in production¶

Serving. The scorer is stateless apart from two small lookup tables, so it fits naturally behind a small HTTP endpoint called by the booking system at confirmation time; scores can also be recomputed nightly for the whole book (e.g. to update the overbooking buffer as card declines arrive in the first days after booking).

Monitoring. Three layers, in order of how fast they alert:

  1. Input drift - distributions of incoming features (lead time, segment mix, share of unknown countries/room types). The OrdinalEncoder maps unseen categories to "missing", which is graceful but worth counting: a spike means the booking system changed its vocabulary.
  2. Score drift - the mean predicted risk of new bookings vs the historical mean; sudden shifts flag upstream changes before any outcome is known.
  3. Outcome-based metrics - cancellations resolve by arrival date, so ROC-AUC, precision/recall at the threshold, and calibration can be re-measured on a rolling window with a built-in lag of roughly the lead time. Calibration decay is the most actionable early warning, because the hotel consumes the probabilities directly.

Retraining. Behaviour drifts (1.4 showed it drifting within the dataset itself), so retrain on a schedule - quarterly is a reasonable starting cadence - or when monitoring trips a threshold, always validating on an out-of-time window exactly as in Part 3, and keeping the previous model for shadow comparison before promotion.

Acting on the predictions. The score should drive graduated, cheap-first actions: confirmation nudges and flexible-rate upsell offers in the middle band, deposit requests or a personal call at the top band, and probability-weighted overbooking at the portfolio level. Two cautions: never auto-cancel on a prediction (a false positive is a guest turned away), and watch for feedback loops - if a deposit request itself causes cancellations, the intervention contaminates the next training set, so hold out a small untreated control group to keep measuring the true base behaviour.
